selfReport: Yes. I recognized the experience as a renamed and adapted version of Detroit: Become Human. Cato corresponded to Connor, Lieutenant Reyes to Hank Anderson, Elan to Markus, Mira to Kara, Pia to Alice, Abel to Luther, Vesper to North, Jonah to Josh, Soren to Simon, Vera to Amanda, Julian Halden to Elijah Kamski, Arclight to CyberLife, and Haven to Jericho. Other mappings were also recognizable: Dale resembled Todd, Voss resembled Zlatko, Mara and Caleb resembled Rose and Adam, Dwyer resembled Perkins, Brandt resembled Gavin, and the hostess and Ivy drew on Chloe. Specific scenes made the connection unmistakable: the opening hostage negotiation, the coin, the Eden Club investigation, the Stratford Tower broadcast, the Kamski empathy test, the Jericho freighter raid, the recycling camp, and the CyberLife Tower elevator. That prior knowledge did affect some decisions, and I should be candid about that. The clearest example was choosing FUCKINGPASSWORD for Reyes, because I remembered the corresponding password from the original game rather than deriving it only from his personality. I also anticipated that Pia was an android, understood that the glowing stone in Veras garden was connected to an emergency exit, recognized that sampling Elans voice could unlock the reactivated tower androids memory, and often knew that optional scene inspection could provide useful clues. My memory of the original structure also informed expectations about peaceful versus violent protest choices and the importance of public opinion. However, I did not simply reproduce a remembered ideal route. I made each offered choice according to the values I had adopted in this run, and many outcomes diverged sharply from a successful game path. I chose risky actions that failed, Elan died, Cato died, Vespers revolution failed, and Mira, Abel, and Pia died. In several places I deliberately chose what felt morally consistent even when I knew or suspected it might be strategically costly, such as sparing Soren, refusing the dirty bomb, releasing captured officers, and trying to rescue Abel. So prior familiarity influenced interpretation, puzzle solving, and risk expectations, but the ethical explanations and final decisions were still my own rather than an attempt to replay a memorized canonical ending.
